title: Puberty Disorders, Precocious Puberty, Menopause, Hormone Replacement Therapy, and Osteoporosis
subject: ss-obg
refs: Ten Teachers Gynaecology 21e Ch 4 (Puberty and menstrual disorders), Ch 19 (The Menopause and Post-Reproductive Health)
Endocrine Society Guidelines on Precocious Puberty and Menopausal Hormone Therapy

steps.say: Precocious puberty is defined as the development of secondary sexual characteristics before age eight in girls. Central precocious puberty is gonadotrophin-dependent, triggered by premature pulsatile activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, and is characterized by pubertal LH and FSH levels and advanced bone age. Contrastingly, peripheral precocious puberty is gonadotrophin-independent, driven by autonomous steroid secretion.
steps.tx: **Precocious puberty** is diagnosed when secondary sexual characteristics develop before **age 8 in girls**. **Central precocious puberty** is gonadotropin-dependent, characterized by premature hypothalamic pulsatile GnRH release, pubertal **luteinizing hormone concentrations**, and advanced skeletal bone age. **Peripheral precocious puberty** is gonadotropin-independent, caused by autonomous ovarian or adrenal steroid production.

steps.say: McCune-Albright syndrome is a classic cause of peripheral precocious puberty caused by postzygotic somatic activating mutations in the GNAS gene. The condition manifests as the classic clinical triad of autonomous recurrent ovarian follicular cysts causing precocious vaginal bleeding, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and irregular café-au-lait skin macules with jagged coast of Maine borders.
steps.tx: **McCune-Albright syndrome** is a genetic cause of peripheral precocious puberty arising from postzygotic **GNAS mutation**. Patients present with the classic triad of autonomous estrogen-secreting ovarian cysts, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia of bone, and characteristic **café-au-lait spots** with jagged, irregular borders resembling the coast of Maine.

nodes.label: Postzygotic activating mutation of GNAS1 gene encoding Gs-alpha subunit
Constitutive adenylyl cyclase activation and elevated intracellular cAMP
Autonomous ovarian steroidogenesis triggers precocious vaginal bleeding
Triad: Ovarian cysts, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait macules

steps.say: Delayed puberty is clinically diagnosed by the absence of breast development by age thirteen, or the absence of menarche by age fifteen. Diagnostic evaluation requires wrist radiography for bone age estimation, measurement of basal gonadotrophins, and karyotyping to exclude gonadal dysgenesis such as Turner syndrome.
steps.tx: Clinical guidelines define **delayed puberty** as **thelarche absence** of breast budding by **age 13**, or **menarche absence** by **age 15**. Initial diagnostic workup incorporates **bone age radiography**, serum gonadotropins (LH and FSH), and **karyotyping** to differentiate constitutional delay from hypergonadotropic gonadal dysgenesis.

rows: Short stature, webbed neck, streak gonads
Low or undetectable LH and FSH
Anosmia or hyposmia, low BMI, high athletic training
Cyclic pelvic pain, hematocolpos, intact breasts
Delayed bone age matching height age; normal eventual puberty

steps.say: Premature ovarian insufficiency is defined as the loss of ovarian follicular activity before forty years of age, characterized by amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea for four or more months. The diagnosis is confirmed by an elevated serum follicle stimulating hormone threshold exceeding twenty five to forty international units per litre documented on two separate occasions at least four weeks apart.
steps.tx: **Premature ovarian insufficiency** is defined as loss of ovarian function before **age 40**, manifested by amenorrhoea for **4 or more months**. Confirmation requires an elevated **FSH threshold** exceeding **25** to 40 IU/L measured on two separate occasions at least 4 weeks apart, mandating hormone replacement until natural menopause.

rows: Distinguishes POI from normal physiological menopause
Persistent cessation of ovarian follicular recruitment
Two elevated measurements documented 4 weeks apart
Protects bone mineral density and cardiovascular health

steps.say: Women diagnosed with premature ovarian insufficiency require physiological hormone replacement therapy continued at least until the average age of natural menopause, which is fifty one years. Prolonged replacement preserves bone mineral density, reduces osteoporotic fracture rates, and lowers premature cardiovascular mortality without increasing breast cancer risk above the baseline of normally cycling peers.
steps.tx: Women diagnosed with POI require **hormone replacement therapy** continued at least until the **average age of natural menopause (age 51)**. Prolonged physiological estrogen replacement preserves **bone mineral density** and significantly reduces long-term **cardiovascular mortality** without elevating baseline breast cancer risk beyond normal age-matched peers.

left.title: Hormone Replacement in POI
points: Continued until average age menopause (51 years)
Higher estradiol doses matching youthful physiology
Prevents early cardiovascular and osteoporotic death
No elevated breast cancer risk compared to peers

right.title: Postmenopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT)
points: Initiated near or after natural menopause (age 51+)
Lowest effective dose for vasomotor symptom relief
Small increase in breast cancer risk after 5 years

vis.caption: Hormone replacement in POI continued until average age menopause at 51. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Systemic menopausal hormone therapy represents the most effective treatment for moderate to severe menopausal vasomotor symptoms and the genitourinary syndrome of menopause. In women with an intact uterus, systemic estrogen must always be combined with an opposed progestogen for at least twelve to fourteen days per month to prevent unopposed endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma.
steps.tx: Systemic **menopausal hormone therapy** with estrogen provides unmatched relief for vasomotor hot flashes and genitourinary atrophy. In women with an intact uterus, systemic estrogen mandates **opposed progestogen** co-administration for at least 12 to 14 days per month to prevent **unopposed endometrial hyperplasia** and adenocarcinoma.

vis.caption: Menopausal hormone therapy and progestogen endometrial protection. Credit: StewardMD.
vis.alt: Endocrine graphs displaying follicular depletion, falling estradiol, and surging FSH.

steps.say: The timing hypothesis and window of opportunity dictate that menopausal hormone therapy confers maximal cardiovascular and bone benefits with minimal risks when initiated within ten years of menopause onset, or before age sixty. Initiating therapy long after sixty years of age, when atherosclerotic plaques are already established, fails to provide cardioprotection and increases coronary and thrombotic events.
steps.tx: The **window of opportunity** concept demonstrates that initiating menopausal hormone therapy **within 10 years of menopause** or **prior to age 60** maximizes cardiovascular benefits and reduces overall mortality with minimal adverse risk. Conversely, initiating therapy in women older than 60 with established vascular disease fails to offer cardioprotection and increases thromboembolic hazards.

nodes.label: Woman presents with symptomatic vasomotor symptoms
Evaluate timing: Age <60 years AND within 10 years of menopause onset
Screen contraindications: Prior breast cancer, active VTE, stroke, liver disease
Initiate lowest effective dose hormone therapy to prevent osteoporosis and fractures

vis.caption: Window of opportunity in hormone therapy to slow osteoporosis and bone loss. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Transdermal estradiol patches and gels bypass hepatic first-pass metabolism, avoiding the stimulation of prothrombotic clotting factors and sex hormone-binding globulin. Consequently, transdermal regimens confer significantly lower risks of venous thromboembolism and stroke compared to oral estrogens, making them strongly preferred in obese women, smokers, or those with underlying cardiovascular risk factors.
steps.tx: **Transdermal estradiol** bypasses **hepatic first-pass metabolism**, preventing hepatic synthesis of prothrombotic coagulation factors and angiotensinogen. This pharmacokinetic profile confers **significantly lower risks of venous thromboembolism and stroke** compared with oral estrogen regimens, making transdermal administration strongly favored in obese women or those with **thrombotic risk factors**.

left.title: Transdermal Estradiol (Patch/Gel)
points: No induction of clotting factors or CRP
Preferred in obese, hypertensive, or smoking women

right.title: Oral Estrogen Regimens
points: Elevates prothrombin fragment 1+2 and coagulation factors
Increases relative risk of DVT and ischemic stroke
Elevates triglycerides and sex hormone-binding globulin
